title: Navigating online misinformation: Understanding older adults' information-seeking behavior in health crises
screen_reason: Survey of 210 Canadian older adults (Qualtrics panel, January 2021) reporting a self-reported frequency-of-encountering-misinformation distribution with shares of respondents (daily 27.62%, weekly 24.29%, less than monthly 20.48%, never 10%). That is a RECALL exposure share with a population denominator. The paper's discernment/accuracy results (belief in true vs false COVID-19 statements) are excluded by the belief rule.

estimates.platform: online survey (Qualtrics panel); online information environment generally
estimates.measure_type: % of older-adult respondents who report encountering perceived COVID-19 misinformation daily
estimates.denominator: 210 Canadian adults aged 60+ recruited from Qualtrics online panels (stratified by age and gender)
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'daily' on the survey question asking how frequently they encounter perceived misinformation about the coronavirus
estimates.misinfo_def: misinformation–that is, false or misleading content that can have significant societal consequences
estimates.source_quote: with (58, 27.62%) encountering it daily and (51, 24.29%) weekly.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own perception of what counts as misinformation; no external verification, no reliability statistics reported
estimates.moderator_quote: Data for this study were collected through an online survey (N = 210), during the month of January 2021, during the second major wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in Canada.
estimates.notes: Frequency scale; the 'daily' category is the highest-frequency threshold reported verbatim. The weekly (24.29%), less-than-monthly (20.48%) and never (10%) categories are other cells of the same distribution; summing daily+weekly to get an 'at least weekly' figure would be a cross-category sum (R8), so only the daily cell is kept. Quote shortened to a contiguous span; the full sentence is split across a page break in the extracted text.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the remaining cells of the same frequency distribution (weekly 24.29%, less than once a month 20.48%, never 10%) — same measure, and combining them would be a cross-category sum barred by R8; the 'never' cell is an absence numerator; (b) discernment/accuracy results (participants correctly identified fewer than half the presented COVID-19 statements; discernment scores) — these are belief/discernment measures, explicitly excluded; (c) verification-behaviour and response shares (67.6% check veracity, 55.24% ignore misinformation, 28.57% consult other sources) — these are behavioural responses to misinformation, not a share of exposure or sharing of misinformation, so not a prevalence estimate; (d) SUS usability score (~66), trust ratings, and the contextual-impact shares (58.71% social restrictions, 11.94% business closures), which are unrelated to misinformation prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, N = 210 Canadians aged 60+, Qualtrics opt-in panel with stratified random sampling by age and gender proportional to Statistics Canada population estimates; fielded January 2021; no response rate reported; misinformation exposure measured by single self-report frequency item, no coder reliability applicable; discernment measured with a set of true/false COVID-19 statements.
rob.item6_quote: misinformation–that is, false or mislead- ing content that can have significant societal consequences
rob.item10_quote: Further, the frequency of encountering perceived misinformation varied as included in Appendix A (Supplementary data) survey instrument (Exposure to the coronavirus misinformation Questions, Question 4), with (58, 27.62%) encountering it daily and (51, 24.29%) weekly.
